nodes.question: How has the theoretical development in sustainability science been characterized according to the text?
nodes.answer: Much theoretical development in sustainability science has focused on meso-level analytical tools, despite recognizing that environmental problems are grand societal challenges.
nodes.paragraph: It has emerged as a field attempting to corral numerous interconnected dis- ciplines and fields of study under an umbrella of scholar - ship that seeks to analyze environmental changes and related concerns, better comprehend the causes and consequences of these concerns, and provide avenues and strategies that encourage socioecological sustainability (Clark 2007; Kates et al. 2001). The last aspect is noteworthy. Scholarship in sustainability science is primarily use inspired (Kates 2011) and illuminates the need for developing and implementing solutions to environmental problems. Despite recognition that many environmental problems constitute grand societal challenges, much theoretical development in the field has focused on meso-level analyti- cal tools (e.g., K hler et al. 2019). In recent years, sustain- ability science has seen a shift toward greater emphasis on transformative change (Sahle et al. 2024a, b), necessitat- ing theories and methods that can expose deeper, structural drivers of sustainability problems and inform strategies to address them (Harnesk and Isgren 2021). Jerneck et al. (2011) were early to make clear that the field must strive to be both problem-solving and critical.

nodes.question: How was the diagnostic approach tested according to the paper?
nodes.answer: The diagnostic approach was tested with four interdisciplinary research teams in sustainability research at Australia's national science agency, CSIRO.
nodes.paragraph: ORIGINAL PAPER Preparing for knowledge co-production: A diagnostic approach to foster re exivity for interdisciplinary research teams E. Ligtermoet1 , C. Munera-Roldan2, C. Robinson1 ,3, Z. Sushil1& P. Leith1 There is broad recognition of the essential requirement for collaboration and co-producing knowledge in addressing sustainability crises and facilitating societal transitions. While mucheffort has focused on guiding principles and retrospective analysis, there is less research onequipping researchers with t-for-context and t-for-purpose approaches for preparing and implementing engaged research. Drawing on literature in co-production, collaboration andtransdisciplinary science, we present an operationalising framework and accompanyingapproach designed as a re exive tool to assist research teams embarking in co-production. This framework encourages critical evaluation of the research contexts in which teams areworking, examining the interactions between positionality, purpose for co-producing, con-textual and stakeholder power, and the tailoring of co-production processes. We tested thisdiagnostic approach with four interdisciplinary research teams preparing for co-production insustainability research in Australia S national science agency, CSIRO. Data collected during and after these applications, indicate that the approach effectively stimulated a greaterunderstanding and application of a critical co-production lens in the research team S engagement planning.
